summary: Describes how a BGP router can check whether the Autonomous System originating a route is actually authorized by the holder of that address prefix. It relies on validated RPKI data and helps reduce accidental or malicious route hijacks, though it only partly addresses the wider problem of BGP security.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6811 defines a way for a BGP router to check whether the network announcing an address prefix is authorized to originate it. The check labels a route Valid, Invalid or NotFound, but it does not verify the complete path the route took.

subtitle: Checks whether the AS originating a BGP prefix is authorized to announce it.

tldr.problem: A BGP route can claim that an Autonomous System originates an address prefix without proving that the prefix holder authorized it.
tldr.mechanism: A router compares the route prefix and origin AS with locally stored Validated ROA Payloads and assigns Valid, Invalid or NotFound.
tldr.outcome: Operators can use the state in route policy, but the check covers only the origin AS and does not validate the full AS path. RFC 6811 has been updated by RFC 8481 and RFC 8893.

facts.label: VRP fields
facts.value: IP address, prefix length, maximum length and origin AS

today: RFC 6811 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 8481 and RFC 8893. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Checking the Origin of a BGP Route
sections.content:
A BGP route associates an address prefix with an AS_PATH, the sequence of Autonomous Systems through which the announcement has travelled. The first AS in the path is the one claiming to originate the prefix. RFC 6811 defines a check of whether that origin AS is authorized by the prefix holder.

The router uses processed prefix-to-AS data, usually from the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI). The RFC does not define how the router obtains its cache data, and it explicitly leaves full AS-path validation out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The check asks whether the AS that originated a route is authorized for its address prefix. It does not check every network listed in the route's path.

sections.title: Validated ROA Payloads and Route Matching
sections.content:
A router stores each validated mapping as a Validated ROA Payload (VRP). A VRP contains an IP address, prefix length, maximum length and origin AS number.

A route prefix is Covered when it is the same as, or more specific than, a VRP prefix. It is Matched when it is Covered, its prefix length does not exceed the VRP maximum length, and its origin AS equals the VRP AS number. The route origin is derived from the final AS_PATH segment using the rules in the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: A VRP records an address range and an AS allowed to originate it. A route matches only when its prefix length and origin AS both fit that record.

sections.title: The Three Validation States
sections.content:
A route is NotFound if no VRP covers its prefix. It is Valid if at least one VRP matches. It is Invalid if one or more VRPs cover the prefix but none matches it.

The result does not depend on the order in which the router checks VRPs. A route origin of NONE cannot match a VRP, and a VRP with AS number zero cannot match a valid route. The router should perform validation on received and redistributed routes; when it does not validate a route, it should initialize the state to NotFound.
sections.plainLanguage: NotFound means there is no covering record. Valid means a record covers the prefix and names the route's origin AS; Invalid means a record covers it but none matches.

sections.title: Route Policy and Cache Changes
sections.content:
Implementations must let operators match and set the validation state in route policy. The state is local route information, not a new BGP attribute, and a router must not discard a route because of the state unless configured to do so. Implementations must support four-octet AS numbers.

When a prefix-to-AS mapping is added or deleted, the router must revalidate affected routes and run its BGP decision process if needed. The RFC describes communication with one or more RPKI caches but leaves the data retrieval protocol to other specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: The validation result is a local property that operators can use in routing policy. When the cached authorization data changes, the router checks affected routes again.

sections.title: How Operators Use Validation
sections.content:
Policy can reject routes marked Invalid or lower their preference, for example by changing LOCAL_PREF. The RFC treats the choice to consider Invalid routes as a local policy decision that requires care.

If a policy decision depends on validation state that is not propagated through IBGP, operators may communicate the state using a community or extended community and set it again at the receiving peer.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators decide whether an Invalid route is rejected or given lower preference. The RFC does not require routers to drop routes automatically.

sections.title: What Origin Validation Cannot Prove
sections.content:
The result depends on the integrity of the database supplying the mappings. If an attacker can add or remove database records, a valid route could be marked Invalid, creating a denial-of-service risk when policy blocks Invalid routes.

The mechanism does not validate the AS path or prevent an attacker from adding the valid origin AS to a forged announcement. The RFC characterizes the mechanism as protection against misconfiguration more than strong security against a determined attacker. Different caches may also contain different data because the distributed RPKI is only loosely consistent.
sections.plainLanguage: This check relies on accurate authorization data and examines only the route origin. It can catch some mistakes, but it cannot establish that every part of a route's path is trustworthy.
